raw.abstractText: The Western diet (WD) is associated with skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism, redox imbalance and inflammation. Emerging evidence suggests that gut microbiome-derived metabolites contribute to host metabolic regulation, yet the role of Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids in skeletal muscle remains unknown. This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD-fed Ldlr<sup>-/-</sup> mice. Male Ldlr<sup>-/-</sup> mice were fed a normal chow or WD and administered L654, L1256 or vehicle control for 8 weeks. Skeletal muscle glycine lipid accumulation, mitochondrial respiration, mitochondrial biogenesis markers, mitophagy-associated signalling, inflammatory and antioxidant proteins and muscle fibre cross-sectional area were assessed. L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle. Functionally, L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid-supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio. L1256 also increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and electron transport chain complexes IV and V, suggesting enhanced oxidative mitochondrial remodelling. In parallel, L1256 altered markers associated with mitochondrial quality control signalling, increased nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), suppressed nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) signalling and preserved muscle fibre cross-sectional area. L654 upregulated mitochondrial biogenesis transcripts without altering protein abundance. These findings identify L1256 as a microbiome-derived lipid retained within skeletal muscle that enhanced oxidative metabolism and preserved mitochondrial quality signalling under metabolic stress. The data suggest that tissue retention of bacterial lipids may be an important determinant of skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation. KEY POINTS: Western diet contributes to skeletal muscle mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired oxidative metabolism and chronic inflammation. Microbiome-derived glycine lipids are bioactive molecules from Bacteroidota species, but their effects on skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism remain poorly understood. Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids produce distinct skeletal muscle responses in Western diet-fed Ldlr<sup>-</sup> <sup>/</sup> <sup>-</sup> mice, where lipid 1256 accumulated in skeletal muscle and enhanced fatty acid-supported respiration, whereas lipid 654 primarily induced transcriptional responses without detectable tissue accumulation. Lipid 1256 increased peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α), mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain together with restoration of Parkin, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) while reducing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) and interleukin 6 (IL-6) expression and preserving skeletal muscle cross-sectional area. These findings suggest that gut microbiome-derived glycine lipids are regulators of skeletal muscle mitochondrial metabolism, and that tissue retention of bacterial lipids influences mitochondrial oxidative remodelling during metabolic stress.

raw.abstractText: How organisms recover from starvation to nutrient-replete physiology remains poorly understood. In C. elegans, we previously observed that transcription factor hlh-30 or a combination of glucose and linoleic acid in its absence are essential for survival with refeeding following starvation, i.e. recovery competence. A forward genetic screen to evaluate mechanisms identified depd-5, which encodes a GATOR1 subunit, loss of which is expected to impair amino acid sensing with unrestrained raga-1 and mTOR activation. Surprisingly, glucose refeeding reduced recovery competence in depd-5(lf, loss-of-function) animals, which was rescued by amino acids, specifically tryptophan. Increasing tryptophan levels in depd-5(lf) worms through supplementation, reduced tryptophan catabolism with tdo-2 ablation and prolonged starvation restored recovery competence. raga-1(gf, gain-of-function) recapitulated whereas raga-1(lf) rescued the impaired recovery competence in starved depd-5(lf) worms. An analogous DEPDC5 mutation in mammalian cells impaired starvation-induced mTOR inactivation. We conclude that tryptophan counters unrestrained mTOR activity to restore recovery competence following starvation.

raw.abstractText:
Objective

Spinal cord stimulation (SCS) is an established therapy for Failed Back Surgery Syndrome (FBSS). The relative long-term performance of tonic low-frequency SCS (LF-SCS) and of combined high-frequency SCS (HFc-SCS), in which 10-kHz and tonic stimulation are delivered simultaneously, remains uncertain. We reviewed our own single-centre experience with both at one and two years.

Methods

Single-centre retrospective cohort study (Cliniques Universitaires Saint-Luc, Brussels). All patients permanently implanted for FBSS since 2019 were reviewed. Twenty-two were eligible: 13 LF-SCS and 9 HFc-SCS. Outcomes were pain (Visual Analogue Scale, VAS), responder rate (≥50% VAS reduction), opioid and neuropathic pain medication use at one and two years, and satisfaction (modified MacNab criteria) and disability (Oswestry Disability Index) at last follow-up. Non-parametric methods were used throughout.

Results

At one year the two modalities were indistinguishable: median VAS reduction differed by 0 points (95% CI -2 to 2), with 85% and 78% responders. At two years (n = 16) the median individual improvement was 50% with LF-SCS and 13% with HFc-SCS (difference 38 percentage points, 95% CI 7 to 66), and 7 of 10 LF-SCS patients remained responders against 0 of 6. Median follow-up differed between groups (57 versus 33 months), a structural confound. Seven of 30 patients trialled developed trial-phase infection (23%); none followed permanent implantation.

Conclusions

In our cohort the two modalities performed equivalently at one year and diverged at two. Given the sample size, unequal follow-up and heterogeneous HFc programming, this divergence is an observation from our practice and is hypothesis-generating.

raw.abstractText:
Background & aims

The liver is a vital metabolic organ with an extraordinary capacity for regeneration, making it a key focus for understanding tissue repair and developing therapeutic strategies for liver diseases. However, ethical limitations restrict liver regeneration research largely to rodents, leaving critical gaps in our understanding of primate-specific mechanisms.

Methods

We performed partial hepatectomy (PHx) using a novel laparoscopically assisted hepatic wedge resection (LAHWR) approach in two cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), one for mechanistic exploration and one for validation. Afterwards, we performed sequential sampling and applied integrative multi-omics approaches, including snRNA-Seq, snATAC-Seq, and spatial transcriptomics (Stereo-Seq), to systematically map cellular and molecular dynamics of primate liver regeneration.

Results

We successfully established two non-human primate models to study the spatiotemporal dynamics of liver regeneration following PHx. We generate a high-resolution map of cellular and molecular dynamics of primate liver regeneration. Our analysis identified a distinct hepatocyte subcluster with fetal liver-like transcriptional features and high regenerative activity emerging in the early stages post-PHx (18.83% in Day 3 vs. 0.48% in Day 0), which predominantly localizes in midlobular zone 2 (P < 0.0001). This subcluster was characterized by elevated expression of proliferation-associated genes and was regulated by key transcription factor POU2F1. Cross-species comparisons revealed that POU2F1 is a primate-specific regulator of liver regeneration, showing significant upregulation in primates (P < 0.01), but not in rodents. Importantly, POU2F1 expression was markedly upregulated in cirrhotic patients (2 for liver samples).

Conclusion

Proliferative hepatocytes localize primarily to midlobular zone 2 during primate hepatectomy regeneration process. POU2F1 is a primate-specific regulator of liver regeneration, implying novel regulatory mechanisms and emphasizing species-specific features.

Impact and implications

The specific mechanisms of liver regeneration in primates remain poorly understood. The hepatocyte population expressing POU2F1 is a hepatocyte cluster with high proliferative capacity, induced after PHx, mainly located in zone 2 of liver lobule. Comparative studies of liver regeneration across species indicate that POU2F1 is a specific regulator in the liver regeneration process of primates. The therapeutic targeting of POU2F1+ hepatocytes is of potential interest in human liver regeneration.

evidenceQuotes: The inter-day profiles of illicit drug residues in wastewater revealed substance-specific and city-dependent temporal patterns, with stimulant drugs and a cocaine metabolite exhibiting suggestive indications of weekend-associated increases.

payload.outcome: A cocaine metabolite showed suggestive indications of weekend-associated increases in wastewater residues, with patterns varying by substance and city.

proposals.rationale: The abstract supports a temporal wastewater pattern for a cocaine metabolite, but does not establish a direct measure of cocaine consumption or a causal explanation.
evidenceQuotes: The inter-day profiles of illicit drug residues in wastewater revealed substance-specific and city-dependent temporal patterns, with stimulant drugs and a cocaine metabolite exhibiting suggestive indications of weekend-associated increases.

payload.effect: CHKA-dependent choline flux supports phosphatidylcholine and platelet-activating factor production; suppressing this flux reduces clonal expansion of mutant hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
models: human HSPCs with endogenous ASXL1 mutations

proposals.rationale: The abstract reports that perturbing CHKA-dependent choline metabolism suppresses clonal expansion and reduces the competitive potential of mutant HSPCs, with effects conserved across ASXL1, DNMT3A, and TET2 models.
evidenceQuotes: Suppressing CHKA-dependent choline flux reduced ASXL1-driven clonal expansion.
Mechanistically, CHKA- dependent choline flux controls phosphatidylcholine production that supports platelet activating factor (PAF) production.
perturbing PAF signaling reduces their competitive potential in an ex vivo clonal competition assay.

payload.claim: Targeting CHKA-dependent choline flux is a mutation-agnostic strategy that suppresses clonal expansion across the three most common clonal hematopoiesis genotypes studied.

proposals.rationale: The abstract explicitly identifies a conserved CHKA/PAF axis and reports suppression of clonal expansion in ASXL1-, DNMT3A-, and TET2-associated models.
evidenceQuotes: This CHKA/PAF axis is conserved in TET2-mutant HSPCs.

Together, these findings identify a mutation agnostic metabolic dependency across the three most common CH genotypes and demonstrate that targeting the CHKA-dependent choline flux suppresses clonal expansion.

proposals.rationale: The abstract mentions choline only as part of the enzyme annotation “glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL)”; it does not report choline as a tested substance, intervention, outcome, or effect.
evidenceQuotes: Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2.

payload.effect: SLC25A32 deficiency sensitized murine and human cancer cells to glycine starvation, suppressed tumor growth during dietary serine/glycine restriction, and impaired metastatic potential in triple-negative breast cancer models.
payload.context: Observed under glycine starvation or dietary serine/glycine restriction in triple-negative breast cancer models with SLC25A32 deficiency.

proposals.rationale: The abstract reports preclinical effects directly involving glycine limitation, but the findings are specific to SLC25A32-deficient triple-negative breast cancer models and should not be generalized beyond this context.
evidenceQuotes: Loss of the folate transporter SLC25A32 sensitized murine and human cancer cells to glycine starvation, suppressed tumor growth during dietary serine/glycine restriction and impaired metastatic potential.
Mechanistically, SLC25A32 deficiency disrupted folate-dependent glycine production, causing glycine auxotrophy, glutathione depletion and oxidative stress.

payload.effect: Combined treatment with glycine and D-cycloserine was strongly synergistic in inhibiting Staphylococcus aureus growth.

proposals.rationale: The abstract directly reports a synergistic growth-inhibitory effect for glycine combined with D-cycloserine.
evidenceQuotes: combined treatment with glycine and the alanine analog antibiotic D-cycloserine was strongly synergistic in inhibiting S. aureus growth.

payload.claim: In Staphylococcus aureus, glycine toxicity is associated with alanine imbalance: glycine inhibits alanine uptake, while D-alanine aminotransferase is required for D-alanine synthesis and tolerance to excess glycine.

proposals.rationale: The abstract identifies alanine uptake inhibition and D-alanine aminotransferase as mechanisms underlying tolerance to excess glycine.
evidenceQuotes: In addition to uptake mechanisms, glycine and diglycine toxicity is neutralized by D-alanine aminotransferase (Dat), which is required for D-alanine synthesis.
The requirement for Dat and DtpT function-but not AapA-in excess glycine is explained by excess glycine inhibiting alanine uptake.

payload.caution: The reported findings concern excess glycine and glycine toxicity mechanisms in Staphylococcus aureus; the abstract does not establish clinical efficacy of glycine as an antibiotic adjuvant in humans.

proposals.rationale: The abstract supports an antibiotic-adjuvant implication but reports bacterial experiments and discusses clinical observations separately without establishing efficacy of the combination in humans.
evidenceQuotes: This study reveals that glycine may be an effective antibiotic adjuvant with D-cycloserine

payload.title: Glycine as a context-dependent excipient in protein-based biopharmaceutical formulations

proposals.rationale: The abstract describes a review critically examining glycine’s physicochemical basis and formulation behavior across liquid, frozen, and freeze-dried protein formulations.
evidenceQuotes: This review critically examines the physicochemical basis and formulation behavior of glycine across liquid, frozen, and freeze-dried systems

payload.effect: Glycine crystallization can support physical robustness and process performance in protein-based biopharmaceutical formulations.

proposals.rationale: The abstract identifies crystallization as a central feature that may provide formulation and process benefits.
evidenceQuotes: crystallization represents a central feature of glycine-containing systems because it can support physical robustness and process performance

payload.caution: Glycine crystallization can create risks of phase separation and loss of local stabilization; outcomes depend on crystallization extent, residual amorphous-phase composition, and the formulation environment.

proposals.rationale: The abstract explicitly describes a benefit-risk balance associated with glycine crystallization and emphasizes its dependence on formulation conditions.
evidenceQuotes: while also creating risks associated with phase separation and loss of local stabilization. This benefit-risk balance depends on the extent of crystallization, the composition of the residual amorphous phase, and the surrounding formulation environment.

payload.claim: Glycine is a multifunctional excipient whose effects are physical-state-, process-, product-, and condition-dependent; use should be supported by direct characterization of physical state and product-specific stability.

proposals.rationale: The review’s overall conclusion cautions against broad stabilization claims and supports product-specific characterization.
evidenceQuotes: Overall, glycine is a multifunctional, physical-state- and process-dependent excipient, and its use should be supported by direct characterization of physical state and product-specific stability.

payload.title: Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids differentially regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation during Western diet feeding in male Ldlr-/- mice
payload.model: male Ldlr-/- mice fed normal chow or Western diet

proposals.rationale: The abstract reports original in vivo findings on two Bacteroidota-derived glycine lipids and skeletal muscle mitochondrial adaptation.
evidenceQuotes: This study tested whether two structurally related bacterial glycine lipids, lipid 654 (L654) and lipid 1256 (L1256), regulate skeletal muscle mitochondrial remodelling in WD-fed Ldlr<sup>-/-</sup> mice.

payload.effect: Enhanced fatty acid-supported skeletal muscle mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio; increased PGC-1α, TFAM, electron transport chain complexes IV and V, Nrf2, MnSOD and GPX4; reduced NF-κB and IL-6 expression; preserved muscle fibre cross-sectional area in Western diet-fed male Ldlr-/- mice.
payload.direction: beneficial mitochondrial and muscle adaptations under metabolic stress

proposals.rationale: L1256 showed tissue accumulation and multiple mitochondrial, antioxidant, inflammatory and muscle-structure effects in the described mouse model.
evidenceQuotes: L1256 selectively enhanced fatty acid-supported mitochondrial respiration and increased respiratory control ratio.

payload.caution: These findings concern the bacterial glycine lipids L654 and L1256, not glycine itself; effects were compound-specific and demonstrated in male Ldlr-/- mice during Western diet feeding.
payload.scope: Do not generalize directly to glycine supplementation or other populations and conditions.

proposals.rationale: The abstract evaluates structurally related bacterial glycine lipids rather than free glycine, and reports different responses for L1256 and L654 in a specific mouse model.
evidenceQuotes: L1256, but not L654, accumulated in skeletal muscle.

proposals.rationale: The abstract does not mention lactoferrin or provide evidence relevant to it.
The abstract concerns spinal cord stimulation modalities for failed back surgery syndrome and contains no evidence about lactoferrin.

payload.title: Spatiotemporal Multi-Omics Reveals Primate-Specific Mechanisms of Liver Regeneration Following Partial Hepatectomy
payload.studyContext: Partial hepatectomy in two cynomolgus monkeys with sequential sampling and integrative single-nucleus and spatial multi-omics

proposals.rationale: This abstract reports a primary non-human-primate study of liver regeneration following partial hepatectomy and is suitable as a new reference.
evidenceQuotes: We performed partial hepatectomy (PHx) using a novel laparoscopically assisted hepatic wedge resection (LAHWR) approach in two cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), one for mechanistic exploration and one for validation.

Afterwards, we performed sequential sampling and applied integrative multi-omics approaches, including snRNA-Seq, snATAC-Seq, and spatial transcriptomics (Stereo-Seq), to systematically map cellular and molecular dynamics of primate liver regeneration.

payload.outcome: A fetal liver-like hepatocyte subcluster with high regenerative activity emerged early after partial hepatectomy and predominantly localized to midlobular zone 2.

proposals.rationale: The abstract reports a quantitative change in a hepatocyte subcluster and its spatial localization during primate liver regeneration.
evidenceQuotes: Our analysis identified a distinct hepatocyte subcluster with fetal liver-like transcriptional features and high regenerative activity emerging in the early stages post-PHx (18.83% in Day 3 vs. 0.48% in Day 0), which predominantly localizes in midlobular zone 2 (P < 0.0001).

payload.claim: POU2F1 was identified as a primate-specific regulator associated with liver regeneration, with significant upregulation in primates but not rodents.
payload.scope: Primate liver regeneration following partial hepatectomy; cross-species comparison

proposals.rationale: The abstract explicitly attributes primate-specific regulatory activity in liver regeneration to POU2F1.
evidenceQuotes: Cross-species comparisons revealed that POU2F1 is a primate-specific regulator of liver regeneration, showing significant upregulation in primates (P < 0.01), but not in rodents.

payload.caution: Findings are based on two cynomolgus monkeys, and the cirrhotic-patient expression observation involved two liver samples; therapeutic relevance remains prospective rather than demonstrated.
payload.scope: Generalizability and translation of the reported liver-regeneration findings

proposals.rationale: The small animal and patient sample sizes limit generalizability, and the abstract describes therapeutic targeting only as being of potential interest.
evidenceQuotes: We performed partial hepatectomy (PHx) using a novel laparoscopically assisted hepatic wedge resection (LAHWR) approach in two cynomolgus monkeys (Macaca fascicularis), one for mechanistic exploration and one for validation.
Importantly, POU2F1 expression was markedly upregulated in cirrhotic patients (2 for liver samples).
The therapeutic targeting of POU2F1+ hepatocytes is of potential interest in human liver regeneration.
